did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title presents it as “A song for the dedication of the house of David,” but the body of the psalm focuses mainly on giving thanks for deliverance, healing, and the transition from distress to joy.
Did you know? David begins by giving thanks that the Lord drew him up—that is, lifted him from a low or dangerous situation—and did not let his enemies rejoice over his downfall.
Did you know? This verse presents two images of salvation together: David describes calling to the Lord and being healed, and in the next verse, being brought up from the grave and restored to life.
Did you know? David does not keep his thanksgiving to himself; he calls on the Lord’s faithful people to sing and give thanks in remembrance of His holiness.

Did you know? The psalm presents a sharp contrast between a moment of anger and a lifetime of God’s favor, and between weeping at night and a shout of joy in the morning—an image of the change from distress to deliverance.
Did you know? David describes how his sense of security in prosperity—“I will never be shaken”—was undermined when he felt that the Lord had hidden His face from him.

Did you know? David asks what benefit there would be in his death and descent into the pit, emphasizing through rhetorical questions that a living person can give thanks to the Lord and proclaim His truth.
Did you know? Deliverance is described through two opposite transformations: mourning is turned into dancing, and sackcloth—the garment of mourning—is replaced with joy.
Did you know? The psalm ends with a personal and enduring commitment: David asks that his “glory” not be silent and declares that he will give thanks to the Lord forever.
